chunks: Why square waves are noisy and how to cut noise. The question: Why are square waves so noisy? What can you do to decrease noise?
What about decreasing noise at a particular frequnecy content?
A square wave jumps from low to high and back almost instantly. Those sudden jumps are the noisy part. A sharp jump holds a lot of fast changes.
Fast changes push strong, brief currents into wires, leak into neighbors, and radiate as radio noise. The best fix is usually to slow the jumps a little.
Think of a hand clap versus a slow handshake. A clap is sudden, so it makes a sharp crackle full of high pitches. A slow, smooth motion makes almost no sound.
A square wave's edge is the clap. Slowing the edge removes the high pitches without changing how often you clap.

Edge: the moment the signal switches from low to high or high to low. Rise time: how long an edge takes. Shorter means sharper.
Harmonic: a sine wave at a whole-number multiple of the signal's repeat rate. A sharp edge needs many high harmonics to build it.
Capacitance: any two nearby conductors act like a tiny bucket that must fill with charge before the voltage changes.
Crosstalk: unwanted signal that leaks from one wire into a neighbor ("Crosstalk").
Take a 10 megahertz clock whose edges take 1 nanoseconds. The clock repeats only 10 million times a second, but each edge is as abrupt as a 350 megahertz wave.
A rule of thumb is 0. 35 divided by the rise time, so real energy reaches the hundreds of MHz.
Now charge a 15 picofarads load (picofarads: tiny, typical of a wire and pin) through 3. 3 volts in 1 nanoseconds.
That takes about 50 milliamps, since current is capacitance times voltage change per second. Stretch the edge to 5 nanoseconds and the surge falls to about 10 milliamps.
That is the whole idea: sharp edge, big brief current, lots of high-frequency energy.
"Square waves are noisy because sharp edges contain a very wide band of harmonics.
On a real board those edges charge capacitance and force current spikes through inductance, which disturbs supplies and grounds, couples into neighbouring traces, and radiates from current loops.
To reduce it, I'd slow the edges, since high harmonics scale as one over rise time, keep loops small over a solid return plane, decouple, filter or ferrite the exits, and use spread-spectrum.
For one frequency I can null it with a duty cycle of one over n or a rise time of one over f, or use a notch or ferrite tuned to it."
